Your GP has checked your ferritin and thyroid — and both came back normal. But normal on a standard panel means above the threshold for disease, not optimal for how you function. Ferritin above 13 ug/L clears the lab range, but optimal for sustained energy is above 70 ug/L. Free T4 is flagged as normal anywhere in a 12-22 pmol/L window, yet many patients feel their best only in the upper third of that range. And fasting insulin — one of the most important metabolic markers for unexplained fatigue — is not routinely tested on NHS panels at all, with optimal sitting below 8 mIU/L. The gap between no disease and optimal function is where private medicine operates.

Testosterone is one of the most underdiagnosed hormonal deficiencies in both men and women — and one of the most impactful to treat. In men, optimal total testosterone is above 15 nmol/L; most labs flag normal from 8.7 nmol/L upward, leaving a large gap where patients experience fatigue, low libido, poor sleep, and cognitive decline. In women, testosterone supports energy, muscle, mood, and sexual function, yet it is almost never tested on standard panels. Private blood testing changes what is possible: find it, understand it, optimise it.

Perimenopause does not start at 50, for many women it begins in their mid-30s, years before periods change. Fluctuating oestrogen and progesterone drive night sweats, anxiety, irregular cycles, brain fog, and fatigue long before any NHS test flags a problem. By the time FSH rises enough to confirm the diagnosis, women have often spent years being told they are fine. Private hormonal panels. FSH, LH ratio, oestradiol, AMH, map exactly where you are in the transition so you can act early, not reactively.

If you are eating less and exercising more but your weight will not shift, the problem is not willpower, it is metabolic. High fasting insulin keeps your body in fat-storage mode regardless of calories. Cortisol dysregulation drives visceral fat accumulation. Sub-optimal thyroid function slows your entire metabolic rate. Insulin resistance prevents cells from using glucose properly. All four are testable and treatable, but none of them appear on a standard NHS review.

One in five people carry elevated Lp(a), a genetically determined lipoprotein that doubles cardiovascular risk independently of LDL, and almost none of them know it, because it is never included in a standard cholesterol panel. Unlike LDL, Lp(a) cannot be lowered by statins, diet, or exercise. It requires specific therapeutic strategies, and you can only act on it if you have tested for it. If you have a family history of early heart disease or stroke, this is the test I would prioritise above everything else.

Insulin resistance can develop silently for a decade before your fasting glucose rises, meaning you can be on the road to type 2 diabetes while your NHS blood test shows entirely normal. The marker that catches it early is fasting insulin: optimal is below 8 mIU/L, but labs do not flag it until 24. Paired with HOMA-IR, you get a ten-year early warning that standard panels simply do not provide. Catch it now and it is reversible. Wait for fasting glucose to rise and the window narrows significantly.

Homocysteine is one of the most consistently underestimated cardiovascular and neurological markers in standard practice. When elevated above 10 µmol/L, it actively damages artery walls, accelerates cognitive decline, and drives peripheral nerve injury, yet it is absent from every standard NHS cholesterol or health check panel. The fix is straightforward: targeted B12, folate, and B6 supplementation usually brings levels down within weeks. Homocysteine is included in the Veridian Cardiovascular Risk Panel alongside ApoB, Lp(a), small dense LDL, and hsCRP, a full picture of what your standard cholesterol result did not show.

The NHS defines vitamin D sufficiency as above 50 nmol/L, which is the level required to prevent rickets. That is a disease prevention threshold, not a health optimisation target. The research on immune function, bone density, mood, and testosterone points to an optimal range of 100 to 150 nmol/L. The average UK adult falls below 50 nmol/L through the winter months, meaning most people are deficient by any meaningful standard. Vitamin D is included in the Veridian Fatigue and Energy Panel alongside thyroid, ferritin, fasting insulin, and B12, the markers that explain why you feel tired even when your standard tests are normal.

Cortisol dysregulation is rarely just about stress. The cortisol awakening response, the sharp rise in cortisol in the 30 to 45 minutes after waking, is a direct readout of how your adrenal system is functioning. A blunted or absent response is associated with fatigue, brain fog, poor recovery from exercise, and low blood pressure. A sustained flat curve through the day often underlies burnout. Morning cortisol is included in the Veridian Energy Screen alongside thyroid, testosterone, fasting insulin, and B12, giving you the complete picture of why your energy is dysregulated.

HbA1c reflects average glucose over three months and only rises once glucose is already substantially elevated. Insulin resistance, the root cause of type 2 diabetes, can be present for a decade while HbA1c reads entirely normal. Fasting insulin catches this years earlier: the body compensates by producing more insulin, so fasting levels creep above the optimal 8 mIU/L long before glucose follows. These two tests together give you a metabolic picture that no standard NHS diabetes screen can provide. Fasting insulin is not a routine NHS test. At Veridian it is included in every metabolic panel.

The omega-3 index measures EPA and DHA levels in red blood cell membranes and is one of the most predictive markers for sudden cardiac death and cognitive decline. An index below 4% carries significant cardiovascular risk; optimal is between 8 and 12%, where membranes are fluid and inflammation is controlled. This is never included in a standard blood panel, and most people have no idea where they sit. Reaching optimal requires either oily fish three times per week or quality supplementation, but you cannot target what you have not measured. This is a test that should be routine.

Vitamin B12 below 500 pmol/L impairs myelin integrity even when labs call it normal above 180. Fasting insulin above 8 mIU/L indicates the metabolic disruption that drives neuroinflammation.
